BUSS1020 Week 08

BUSS1020 Week 8 — One-Sample Hypothesis Testing

Statistical inference

Descriptive statistics summarise observed data through quantities such as the mean, median and mode and displays such as bar charts, histograms and boxplots. Inferential statistics use a random sample to learn about fixed but unknown population parameters. Estimation gives a point estimate or confidence interval; hypothesis testing evaluates evidence against a specified parameter claim.

A confidence interval has the form point estimate ± critical value × standard error. A test statistic has the related form (estimate − hypothesised parameter value)/standard error under the null model. Standardisation measures how far the observed estimate is from the null value in sampling-error units.

Hypotheses and direction

The null hypothesis H₀ specifies the benchmark being tested. The alternative H₁ states the research question. These need not literally be an old and a new theory: their statistical roles are the null model and the departure under investigation.

For a population mean μ and benchmark μ₀:

Research question

Boundary null used in calculation

Alternative

Tail

Is the mean different?

μ = μ₀

μ ≠ μ₀

Two-sided

Has the mean increased?

μ = μ₀

μ > μ₀

Upper

Has the mean decreased?

μ = μ₀

μ < μ₀

Lower

For a directional test, the full null can include μ ≤ μ₀ or μ ≥ μ₀. Calculation uses the equality boundary μ = μ₀. Equality belongs to the null, not the alternative. Choose the direction before looking at the results. Replace μ with π and μ₀ with π₀ when testing a population proportion.

Decisions, errors and power

Decision

H₀ is true

H₀ is false

Fail to reject H₀

Correct; probability 1 − α

Type II error; probability β

Reject H₀

Type I error; probability α

Correct; probability 1 − β

The significance level α is the probability of rejecting a true null under the specified testing procedure. β is the probability of failing to reject for a particular false-null parameter value. Power = 1 − β is the probability of detecting that departure.

For a fixed design and effect, raising α generally lowers β. This is a trade-off, not a literal inverse-proportion equation. Larger samples can improve power without raising α. Other things equal, power increases with effect size and sample size and decreases with noise. If H₀ specifies μ = 50 but the true mean is 60, a larger separation makes the departure easier to detect.

In interval estimation, 1 − α is the repeated-sampling coverage of the interval procedure. In a test, it is the probability of not rejecting when H₀ is true. Neither is the probability that H₀ itself is true.

The p-value

The p-value is the probability, assuming H₀, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed statistic in the direction or directions specified by H₁. It is not P(H₀ is true). Smaller values indicate stronger incompatibility with H₀.

The p-value depends on the data, null model and alternative, including whether the test is one- or two-sided. It does not depend on the α chosen for the decision. It is the threshold significance level at which the test would reject, subject to the convention used at equality.

Three decision methods

Critical values: for a symmetric Z or t distribution, reject an upper-tail test above the positive 1 − α percentile, a lower-tail test below the α percentile, or a two-sided test when the statistic's absolute value exceeds the positive 1 − α/2 percentile.

p-value: reject when p-value < α; otherwise fail to reject.

Confidence interval: a two-sided test rejects when its null value lies outside the matching 1 − α interval. The method and standard error must match. A central 95% two-sided interval is not the general counterpart of a one-sided 5% test.

Matching procedures give the same decision. Reporting a p-value allows readers to compare the evidence with different α values. Statistical significance must be distinguished from practical importance. Failing to reject does not prove the null.

Choosing and calculating a test

Let n be sample size, x̄ the sample mean, σ the known population standard deviation, s the sample standard deviation, X the success count and p̂ = X/n the sample proportion. Standard error, abbreviated SE, describes sampling variation rather than variation of individual observations.

Test

Statistic

Reference distribution

Mean, σ known

z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n)

Standard normal

Mean, σ unknown

t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n)

Student t with df = n − 1

Proportion

z = (p̂ − π₀)/√[π₀(1 − π₀)/n]

Approximate standard normal

For the mean, random independent observations from a normal population give an exact normal sample mean. Using s gives the exact t reference under that normal model. For appropriate non-normal populations, large-sample inference is approximate; n ≥ 30 is a practical guideline rather than a guarantee against severe skewness or influential observations.

The t distribution is symmetric, has heavier tails than the standard normal, and approaches it as df increases. Its mean exists and equals 0 for df > 1; its variance equals df/(df − 2) for df > 2. Degrees of freedom are a shape parameter, not the sample standard deviation.

Under independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability π, X has a binomial distribution. The proportion X/n has a scaled-binomial distribution on {0, 1/n, …, 1}, not an ordinary binomial count distribution. For the proportion test, assess nπ₀ ≥ 5 and n(1 − π₀) ≥ 5. Use π₀ in the null standard error; it is the null model that determines the test's sampling distribution.

For sampling without replacement from a finite population of N units, multiply the standard error by √[(N − n)/(N − 1)] when the sampling fraction warrants a finite-population correction, commonly n/N > 0.05. If the finite population size is not supplied, no such numerical correction can be calculated; this does not literally establish that the population is infinite.

A complete testing procedure

Define the population parameter and state H₀ and H₁.

Choose α before inspecting the outcome.

Plan the sample size and sampling design.

Select the test and check its assumptions.

Specify the null reference distribution and decision rule.

Collect the data and calculate the statistic and p-value.

State the statistical decision and interpret the research question in context.

Use “reject H₀” or “fail to reject H₀” for the decision. A conclusion states whether there is sufficient evidence for the alternative; it does not claim that a hypothesis has been proved.

Worked examples

Case A — Bolt diameter, known σ

The claimed mean diameter is 30, σ = 0.8, n = 100, x̄ = 29.84 and α = 0.05. Test H₀: μ = 30 against H₁: μ ≠ 30.

SE = 0.8/√100 = 0.08.

z = (29.84 − 30)/0.08 = −0.16/0.08 = −2.00.

The two-sided critical values are ±1.96; |z| = 2.00 > 1.96.

p-value = 2P(Z ≤ −2) ≈ 0.0455, or about 0.0456 using rounded tail probabilities.

Reject H₀. There is evidence that the true mean differs from 30. The negative estimate difference indicates that the observed departure is downward; the prespecified test remains two-sided.

Case B — New York hotel prices, unknown σ

A claim gives a mean nightly price of $168. A random sample of n = 25 hotels has x̄ = $172.50 and s = $12. Test H₀: μ = 168 against H₁: μ ≠ 168 at α = 0.05. With this small sample, validity requires an appropriate approximately normal population model.

SE = 12/√25 = $2.40.

t = (172.50 − 168)/2.40 = 4.50/2.40 = 1.875.

df = 24; the critical values are ±2.0639.

Two-sided p-value = 2P(T₂₄ ≥ 1.875) ≈ 0.073.

Fail to reject H₀: there is insufficient evidence of a mean different from $168. The matching interval calculated from these data is 172.50 ± 2.0639(2.40) = $167.55 to $177.45, which contains $168.

Case C — Marketing response proportion

A company claims an 8% response rate. In n = 500 randomly selected recipients, X = 25 respond. Test H₀: π = 0.08 against H₁: π ≠ 0.08 at α = 0.05.

Null expected counts: 500(0.08) = 40 and 500(0.92) = 460, both at least 5.

p̂ = 25/500 = 0.05.

Null SE = √(0.08 × 0.92/500) = 0.012133.

z = (0.05 − 0.08)/0.012133 ≈ −2.47.

|z| > 1.96 and the two-sided p-value is approximately 0.0136.

Reject H₀. The response proportion differs from 8%, with the observed sample proportion below the claim. No finite population size is specified for a correction.

Amazon upper-tail mean test

For H₀: μ = 50 against H₁: μ > 50, α = 0.10 and n = 25, take the supplied test statistic t = 1.55 with df = 24. The upper critical value is 1.3178, so 1.55 > 1.3178. The one-sided p-value is about 0.067, below 0.10: reject H₀ and conclude evidence of a mean above 50.

Coca-Cola positive-response threshold

Of n = 100 people, 8 respond positively. To establish a response rate above 10%, use H₀: π ≤ 0.10 and H₁: π > 0.10, calculating at π₀ = 0.10.

p̂ = 0.08, SE = √(0.10 × 0.90/100) = 0.03, and z = (0.08 − 0.10)/0.03 = −0.67. At α = 0.05, the upper critical value is +1.645. The upper-tail p-value is approximately 0.7475. Fail to reject: these data do not establish a rate above 10%. A profitability threshold requires evidence in the chosen direction, not merely any difference from 10%.

Excel calculations

• NORM.S.INV(q) returns the standard normal percentile with left cumulative probability q.

• NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE) returns the left-tail probability.

• Two-sided normal p-value: 2*NORM.S.DIST(-ABS(z),TRUE).

• Upper-tail normal p-value: 1-NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE); lower-tail: NORM.S.DIST(z,TRUE).

• T.INV(q,df) returns a left-cumulative t percentile; T.INV.2T(alpha,df) returns the positive two-sided critical magnitude.

• T.DIST(t,df,TRUE) returns a left-tail probability.

• T.DIST.2T(ABS(t),df) returns the two-sided t p-value. Use the absolute statistic, including zero when relevant.
